title: Hazamir, Muze, and the Cultural Stage of Będzin
summary: Music, drama, literature, and public performances gave Będzin’s residents a lively cultural world alongside politics and religious life.

editorialContent:
![Będzin, the town whose Jewish cultural life Hazamir and Muze helped shape](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/B%C4%99dzin_-_Zamek_obronny_z_XIVw..jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)
## From political circles to a cultural home

In 1907, after the Russian Revolution of 1905–06 had been crushed and political activity faced severe repression, a group of young people in Będzin turned toward cultural work. The memorial book identifies [Hazamir](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_c62181de27ef46b091e8eacf) as the association they created: a music, literary, and dramatic society whose name means “the nightingale.” The book names Jakob Krygsztajn, Hershl Shtrochlic, Kopel Openhajm, and Ruwen Sączow among its founders, alongside Isidor Lewinski. It recalls the association as more than a club: a meeting place for young people and older members of the town’s Jewish national and working intelligentsia.

The founders’ cultural choice should not be mistaken for proof that they had left politics behind. Rather, the book presents Hazamir as a way to sustain shared life when political work was constrained. Its choir and orchestra rehearsed several times a week in the Harmonie hall on Słowiańska Street, now Małachowski. The first concert, staged with a Purim ball, was remembered as a public celebration. Local women and men sang and played; the association offered a place to learn, perform, and gather in Yiddish culture.

The wider setting helps explain the ambition. Będzin was a major Jewish town in the industrial Zagłębie region. The 1921 census counted 17,298 Jews—about 62 percent of its population, according to the town’s [Wikipedia history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C4%99dzin). Hazamir’s organizers were building for a large and varied public, not a small private circle. The memorial book places its beginnings in a moment when associations could link cultural activity to Jewish collective identity without being reducible to one political party.

## A choir, a library, and visiting writers

Hazamir’s strongest musical period, as the memorial book tells it, came under Leon Kopf, a young musician who had completed musical studies abroad. The choir grew to 49 women and men and performed demanding works by Handel, Louis Lewandowski, Meyerbeer, and Mendelssohn. The account’s praise reflects a survivor’s memory, not an independent assessment of the ensemble’s standard; still, its detail conveys the seriousness with which the association approached amateur performance.

Finances proved a persistent weakness. By the end of 1912, Kopf had left, and the celebrated composer Matityahu Bensman took over. The book says Bensman organized concerts of Jewish folk music and theater performances, and rehearsed Verdi’s *La Traviata* in Yiddish in his own poetic translation, before leaving Będzin too. The contrast is striking: the association reached for ambitious repertoire, yet depended on limited local resources and the commitment of individual artists.

Hazamir also made a literary stage. The memorial book dates the opening of its library to 20 December 1913, with Yiddish writer I. L. Peretz invited to speak. Its account of Peretz’s visit differs in emphasis from another recollection in the same book: one passage links him to the opening of a “Sholem Aleichem Library,” while the Hazamir chapter calls it the Hazamir Library. The later name may reflect a subsequent dedication, but the supplied text does not settle the naming history. The remembered event, however, is clear: a crowded evening of readings and a celebration of Yiddish literature.

The book also gives a vivid account of Sholem Aleichem’s visit in summer 1914, shortly before the First World War. A Hazamir delegation met him and his wife at the station; the Corso theater hall filled for his readings. A separate record places Abraham Reisin’s visit in late 1910, as Hazamir’s guest at an artistic evening. These episodes made the town part of a wider circuit of Yiddish literary life: celebrated writers came to meet audiences, while local organizers provided the hall, welcome, and public occasion.

## From amateur theater to Muze

Drama had been part of Hazamir’s work, but the memorial book describes a gradual division of labor. An earlier [Scenic Amateur Circle](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_c1bfe28ab5fce3ac1333839b) staged plays including [*Dodem Fidele*](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_fd8df993c8da54c4d88f1e04), [*Yidn*](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_f1022f37d46743b8f7b20761), [*Family Tzvi*](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_30884eea583af24960bba74e), and [*The Wild Man*](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_b7e3e6679172e7c1d570d16f). Its dramatic circle drew on works by Sholem Aleichem and Sholem Asch, among others. The book recalls local performers including the Fersztenfeld sisters, Hershl Shtatler, Herman Shtrochlic, Lejbl Goldsztajn, Dawid Pinkus, and Majer Cymberknopf.

On 7 May 1921, the [Jewish Dramatic Society Muze](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_b94982f8df3e95c366758bf6) held its official founding meeting at the Haka Association premises. The surviving account links Muze to earlier amateur circles and says the new society concentrated more heavily on drama, while Hazamir continued its musical and literary activity. H. Stattler—also rendered H. Shtatler in the records—led Muze; its named members included A. Weinstock, H. Wekselman, W. Rechnitz, E. Blumenfrucht, H. Leber, and Israel Lasker. The spelling variation warns against assuming that every similar name in separate records identifies the same person.

Visiting performers brought professional theater into contact with that local stage. In 1921, Esther Rachel Kamińska’s troupe presented *The Dybbuk* in Będzin, with Ida Kamińska as Lea and Esther Rachel as Frajda. The memorial book says young Muze actors were invited to take small parts and that Kamińska encouraged them when she saw their nervousness. It remembers two full performances and an autograph dedication wishing one young actor success on the Jewish stage. The testimony makes the visit more than a touring engagement: it shows a meeting between an established theatrical company and performers still finding their footing.

## A living stage, not a single society

The memorial book’s account reaches beyond the founding years. It recalls later connections between Będzin and theatrical artists, including Feder’s work with Jacob Ratboym’s studio on *Nothing Changes in the World* in 1934, and Feder’s return to Zagłębie in 1935 to contact the town’s drama society. It also names David Herman in connection with Muze. The book identifies him as a well-known director, but does not provide enough detail to reconstruct precisely the extent or dates of his local involvement. Likewise, it names Moshe Potashinsky among performers who emerged from Muze’s dramatic studio; the supplied records do not establish a complete biography or settle the different transliterations attached to his name.

These associations belonged to a broader Jewish cultural world in which amateur societies, touring companies, writers’ appearances, and professional stages overlapped. The [YIVO Encyclopedia’s entry on the Warsaw Yiddish Art Theater](https://yivoencyclopedia.org/article.aspx/Warsaw_Yiddish_Art_Theater) describes the success of *The Dybbuk* in Warsaw in 1920 as evidence of a substantial audience for serious Yiddish drama in Poland. That context helps explain why a Będzin society could aspire to more than occasional entertainment: audiences were part of a culture with active artistic companies and a repertoire traveling between towns.

The independent record adds a boundary to the story as well as context. Yad Vashem’s [Encyclopedia of the Ghettos entry for Będzin](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=150) documents the persecution and deportations that destroyed the town’s Jewish community in 1942–43. It does not independently verify Hazamir’s concerts, Muze’s productions, or the individual performances described by survivors. Those details remain the memorial book’s testimony and should be read as such—not dismissed for lacking outside corroboration, but not presented as independently confirmed.

Hazamir and Muze left a memory of cultural work carried by named people: organizers, singers, amateur actors, conductors, librarians, and visitors. Their stage connected Będzin to Yiddish literature and theater beyond the town, while giving local performers a place to speak and sing for their neighbors. The record invites further research into the [Harmonie hall on Słowiańska Street](research:Hazamir rehearsals at the Harmonie hall on Słowiańska Street), the identities of the [Fersztenfeld sisters](research:the Fersztenfeld sisters of Będzin’s amateur theater), and the later careers of Muze performers such as Moshe Potashinsky. These are open questions, not gaps to be filled by guesswork.
